[0] The input already contains Chinese text. Here is the English translation:

[1] The judgment states that the Alliance continued to publish its aims, political propositions and ideology through its website, YouTube clips, etc. (Screenshot)

[2] Website content: Linking June Fourth with the anti-extradition movement to rally protestors and grow the ranks

[3] The judge held that from 1991 onwards, and even after the state amended the Constitution and the National Security Law took effect, the Alliance adopted and advocated the "end one-party dictatorship" slogan at its June Fourth vigils; its actual words and deeds revealed the "nature" of its activities more than its articles of association.

[4] The judgment notes that the Alliance's website, YouTube channel, the "June Fourth Memorial Museum" website and the like continuously published the Alliance's aims, political propositions and ideology. The court considered the most relevant to this case to be the online exhibition titled "Shared Fate, Joint Struggle — 'The 1989 Pro-Democracy Movement and Hong Kong'" and the exhibition titled "On the Frontline Against Authoritarianism — From 'June Fourth' to the Anti-Extradition Movement". The court held that the Alliance was trying to link June Fourth with the social climate in Hong Kong at the time — "a concrete example of its attempt to rally or attract local protestors to join and grow its ranks".

[5] The judge held that by linking June Fourth with the anti-extradition movement, the Alliance sought to "plant" in supporters' minds the idea of ending one-party dictatorship, and to encourage them to put it into practice. (File photo)

[6] The judge noted that it is "common knowledge" that the "anti-extradition" incidents at the time were not limited to criticism of the government, but involved large-scale unlawful protest activities. Given the social atmosphere of the time, by "combining" June Fourth with the anti-extradition movement, the Alliance was not only seeking to "plant" in supporters' minds the idea of ending one-party dictatorship, but also to encourage them to put it into practice.

[7] The judgment also referred to the June Fourth Memorial Museum website, noting that it preserves relevant individuals' memories of the June Fourth incident, allowing those who had attended the vigil to revisit the content — including the "end one-party dictatorship" message — and those who had not attended to receive the same text-based information.

[8] The judgment cited the Alliance's social media posts, including Szeto Wah's 2004 speech in the Legislative Council. (File photo)

[9] Facebook and Twitter: Amplifying the reach of the Alliance's activities

[10] The court noted that the Alliance used Facebook and Twitter (now X) to spread its message more widely and rapidly than its website, amplifying the effect of its physical activities. The judgment cited several posts, including a 1 July 2020 Facebook post titled "The National Security Law — Trampling Human Rights and the Rule of Law, Destroying One Country Two Systems", which said: "In the face of the National Security Law, #the Alliance's position remains unchanged. We will continue to uphold our five major goals, resist one-party dictatorship, preserve the memory of June Fourth, and support China's democratic movement. However, faced with increasingly severe risks, we must also have contingency plans and prepare for a long-term struggle...."

[11] The court held that this clearly showed the Alliance persisted in "ending one-party dictatorship" after the National Security Law took effect, and anticipated that some supporters would put the slogan into practice — even if non-violently, they might still constitute "other unlawful means" under the National Security Law, hence the "increasingly severe" risks it faced.

[12] Another Alliance post, titled "Never forget the June Fourth incident — Rehabilitate the 1989 pro-democracy movement", quoted Szeto Wah's 2004 Legislative Council speech: "Chinese officials believe the Alliance would have to give up the 'end one-party dictatorship' slogan before they would talk to the democrats who participate in the Alliance.... The so-called 'dialogue' is nothing more than wanting us to live forever under 'one-party dictatorship', to give up the pursuit of democracy and freedom, and to be obedient citizens."

[13] The court held that the post represented the consistent position of the Alliance and all defendants, and that its reiteration after the National Security Law took effect was clearly intended to tell the public that it would maintain its stance as always and would not abandon its line of struggle in pursuit of dialogue with the central government. Given the Alliance's refusal to communicate with Beijing, the court did not accept that the standing committee members genuinely hoped to push for constitutional amendment to achieve "ending one-party dictatorship".

[14] The court noted that the June Fourth Memorial Museum provided promotional items featuring a stylised "Hong Kong / Add Oil" design, with the aim of rallying social movement protesters to join and grow the ranks. (File photo)

[15] June Fourth Memorial Museum: Promotional items feature the familiar protest-style "Hong Kong / Add Oil" design

[16] The judgment stated that the physical June Fourth Memorial Museum was open to the public, with the operating aim of spreading the Alliance's political stance to the public and serving as a venue for events such as press conferences. The judge noted that the museum allowed the public to visit at a fixed location over the long term and thereby come into contact with information related to the Alliance and "ending one-party dictatorship", as evidenced by files recovered from a police-seized USB drive.

[17] The judge further noted that the promotional items provided by the museum, besides carrying the slogan "end one-party dictatorship", some featured the "Hong Kong / Add Oil" design commonly seen in Hong Kong social movement protests. The judge believed that beyond promoting "ending one-party dictatorship", the Alliance also hoped that its protest-themed promotional items could rally or attract local social movement protesters to join and grow its ranks.

[18] The dissolved Alliance, as a legal person, was listed as the first defendant in the case; the judge held that the Alliance could be prosecuted and, if convicted, punished. (File photo)

[19] "Co-conspirator" statements

[20] The court said it had considered the "co-conspirator rule" in deciding whether co-conspirator statements could be admitted as evidence, accepting Chow Hang-tung's submission that if a speaker made statements in the capacity of the Alliance's chair, vice-chair or standing committee member, those statements represented the Alliance's position. The judge said that although the defendants disputed that some statements did not represent the Alliance, this was not a decisive consideration, as the content in question did not differ materially from the defendants' stance.

[21] The court said that when applying the "attribution principle", it carefully considered whether the words and deeds of the three defendants reflected the Alliance's "dominant intent", such that the intentions and conduct found unlawful by the court could be treated as those of the Alliance. Having considered a number of statements made when some defendants were not present under the "co-conspirator rule", the court ultimately ruled that the defendants had engaged in "joint criminality".
